title: High-rate Multipartite Quantum Secret Sharing With Composable Security
authors: Russell M. J. Brooks, Joseph Ho, Joseph Niblo, Janka Memmen, Anna Pappa, Jens Eisert, Nathan Walk, Alessandro Fedrizzi
abstract: ArXiv:2609.13367v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Future quantum communication networks will conceivably support cryptographic tasks that require entanglement among more than two users. Quantum secret sharing is a prime example where entanglement provides a direct means to coordinate untrusted parties with security from eavesdropping in a multi-party setting. However, the canonical GHZ-based protocols can be vulnerable to participant attacks, in which untrusted parties try to learn the secret without collaborating. Here, we experimentally evaluate a discrete-variable [MATH]-threshold quantum secret-sharing protocol whose finite-key analysis provides composable security against general attacks, including participant attacks. Using two domain-engineered entangled photon pair sources, we generate 4-qubit GHZ states at rates above [MATH] fourfold events per second and a maximum asymptotic secret key rate of [MATH] bits per second. We then distribute the state through a 4-arm star network comprising 20\~km of fibre in total. From the measured event rates and error statistics, we infer that a randomised 24-hour execution with the optimised basis probability would yield a composable finite-key lower bound of 8.7 Mbits, under the assumption that the measured source and device statistics remain stationary.
tldr: This work experimentally demonstrates a high-rate four-party threshold quantum secret-sharing protocol with composable finite-key security against general and participant attacks over a 4-arm star fibre network.
motivation: Future quantum networks require multi-party cryptographic tasks, but canonical GHZ-based secret sharing can be vulnerable to participant attacks, motivating protocols with composable security guarantees in realistic network settings.
method: The authors use two domain-engineered entangled photon pair sources to generate 4-qubit GHZ states, distribute them through a 4-arm star network with 20 km of fibre, and apply a finite-key analysis for composable security against general attacks including participant attacks.
result: They obtain fourfold event rates above threshold and a maximum asymptotic secret key rate, inferring a composable finite-key lower bound of 8.7 Mbits for a randomised 24-hour execution under stationary statistics.
conclusion: The experiment shows that high-rate multipartite quantum secret sharing with strong composable security is feasible over a small-scale fibre network, advancing practical multi-party quantum communication.

title: No Cardinality Bound For Squashed Entanglement
authors: Graeme Smith Rabsan Galib Ahmed
abstract: ArXiv:2609.14031v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Squashed entanglement is an additive bipartite entanglement measure. For a state [MATH], it is defined as the infimum of all conditional mutual information [MATH] evaluated on extensions [MATH]. It was unresolved whether there is a bound on the dimension of the conditioning system, [MATH], needed for this optimization. We show that no such cardinality bound is possible. Explicitly, we find that the squashed entanglement for a partially dephased Bell pair on two qubits cannot be achieved for any finite dimensional extension [MATH]. A crucial ingredient of this proof is a direct sum step, which in a sense, symmetrizes two purifying systems while keeping the conditional mutual information unchanged and the coherence no worse.
tldr: The paper proves that squashed entanglement cannot be achieved with any finite-dimensional conditioning system by showing a partially dephased Bell pair on two qubits requires an infinite-dimensional extension.
motivation: Squashed entanglement is an additive entanglement measure defined as an infimum of conditional mutual information over extensions, and it was unresolved whether the dimension of the conditioning system could be bounded.
method: The authors use a direct sum construction that symmetrizes two purifying systems while keeping the conditional mutual information unchanged and the coherence no worse, then apply it to rule out finite-dimensional achieving extensions.
result: For a partially dephased Bell pair on two qubits, the squashed entanglement cannot be attained by any finite-dimensional extension, establishing that no cardinality bound exists.
conclusion: This settles a longstanding question about squashed entanglement and reveals that infinite-dimensional conditioning systems can be necessary in entanglement measures.

title: High Quantum Local Differential Privacy Breaks Entanglement
authors: Sujeet Bhalerao, Theshani Nuradha, Felix Leditzky
abstract: ArXiv:2609.13418v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Differential privacy provides a mathematical framework for guaranteeing privacy for sensitive data. In quantum information processing, the interaction of privacy constraints with quantum resources such as entanglement remains a question of interest. Given that the utility of many protocols, and often the presence of a quantum advantage, relies on quantum resources such as entanglement, it is crucial to understand when a privacy requirement for a quantum channel is compatible with the channel's ability to preserve entanglement. We study this question for quantum local differential privacy (QLDP). Our main result shows that every [MATH]-QLDP channel with a [MATH]-dimensional input is entanglement-breaking whenever [MATH]. We also prove an approximate version for [MATH]-QLDP, where channels in the same high-privacy regime are close in diamond norm to an entanglement-breaking channel. We further prove a composition result for a collection of private quantum channels having entangled inputs and global measurements in the high-privacy regime. Finally, we apply our results to private quantum learning theory. We prove that any learning protocol using arbitrary quantum memory on copies of the output of an entanglement-breaking channel can be simulated by a protocol that measures the corresponding unprocessed input copies one at a time while storing only classical information. Combining this result with our high-privacy entanglement-breaking theorem, we show that under sufficiently private local noise, a learning protocol with quantum memory for purity testing and bipartite product testing is subject to the sample complexity lower bounds for protocols with single-copy measurements on the noiseless tasks. We also obtain stronger sample complexity lower bounds when a single highly private channel acts on the entire multipartite input.
tldr: The paper proves that quantum channels satisfying high local differential privacy must be entanglement-breaking, with applications to private quantum learning and sample complexity lower bounds.
motivation: Privacy constraints in quantum information processing may conflict with the entanglement needed for quantum advantages, so it is important to understand when privacy requirements are compatible with entanglement preservation.
method: The authors analyze ε-quantum local differential privacy (QLDP) channels, prove exact and approximate entanglement-breaking thresholds, establish a composition result for private channels with entangled inputs, and simulate quantum-memory learning protocols using classical memory.
result: Every sufficiently private QLDP channel with d-dimensional input is entanglement-breaking; approximately private channels are close in diamond norm to entanglement-breaking channels, and private learning protocols with quantum memory are subject to single-copy measurement sample complexity lower bounds.
conclusion: High local differential privacy fundamentally breaks entanglement and restricts quantum memory advantages in learning tasks, linking privacy to operational limitations in quantum information processing.

motivation: The Wigner Shannon entropy conjecture posits a lower bound on the entropy of Wigner-positive states, and counterexamples would clarify fundamental constraints on phase-space information measures.
method: The authors provide explicit finite-energy counterexamples, rank-two finite-Fock-support families with analytic positivity and entropy bounds, and optimize over one-mode Wigner-nonnegative states with bounded mean photon number.

The authors construct explicit finite-energy counterexamples, including rank-two finite-Fock-support families with analytic positivity and entropy bounds. For fixed Fock level n and coherence fraction 0≤λ<1, they derive the entropy difference h(W)-(1+lnπ) = (2n-2^n λ^2)t^2 + O_{n,λ}(t^4), yielding finite-support counterexamples for every n≥3 above an explicit coherence threshold. They also show that a vanishing quadratic term does not prevent entropy descent: a fully coherent vacuum–one-photon core with vanishing positive thermal repair gives h(W)-(1+lnπ) = -4t^6/3 + o(t^6). For the vacuum–three-photon construction, they determine the logarithmic asymptotic of the minimum fixed-thermal mixing weight required for Wigner nonnegativity. Finally, optimizing over all one-mode Wigner-nonnegative states with mean photon number at most E, they prove that the maximal entropy deficit scales as E^γ/[ln(1/E)]^β with γ≈0.7412033679 and β≈0.5861054961, showing that the vacuum entropy is recovered as E→0 but the optimal deficit decays much more slowly than any universal linear correction in the mean energy.

title: An Entropic Characterization Of Haag Duality
authors: Lauritz van Luijk Ruizhi Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.13550v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Motivated by Haag duality in quantum spin systems, we show that Haag duality for a pair of commuting factors generated by increasing sequences of finite-dimensional matrix algebras is equivalent to the asymptotic vanishing of a suitable conditional mutual information. For two-dimensional spin systems, let an annulus separate a finite region from the exterior. Haag duality then holds for a region [MATH] if and only if the mutual information of the inner region and the exterior, conditioned on the part of [MATH] inside the annulus, vanishes as the outer radius becomes large. As a corollary, assuming a strict area law with subleading corrections, Haag duality holds for single cones, and it holds for unions of two or more disjoint cones precisely when the topological entanglement entropy vanishes. For translation-invariant pure states on spin chains, half-chain Haag duality is equivalent to vanishing entropy density.
tldr: Haag duality for commuting factors in quantum spin systems is shown to be equivalent to the asymptotic vanishing of a conditional mutual information, linking it to area laws and topological entanglement entropy.
motivation: Haag duality is a foundational structural property of local quantum systems, but its information-theoretic meaning and its connection to entanglement structure were not fully understood.
method: The authors characterize Haag duality for increasing sequences of finite-dimensional matrix algebras as equivalent to the vanishing of a suitable conditional mutual information, and analyze annulus-separated regions in two-dimensional spin systems and half-chains in translation-invariant spin chains.
result: Haag duality for a region holds iff the mutual information between the inner region and the exterior, conditioned on the annulus, vanishes asymptotically; under a strict area law with subleading corrections, it holds for single cones and for unions of cones precisely when topological entanglement entropy vanishes, and for spin-chain half-chains it is equivalent to vanishing entropy density.
conclusion: The work provides an entropic, information-theoretic reformulation of Haag duality that ties it to entanglement measures, area laws, and topological entanglement entropy.

title: Hiai--Petz Skew Informations And Sharp Uncertainty Relations For A Single Observable
authors: Gen Kimura
abstract: ArXiv:2609.13870v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study intrinsic quantum uncertainty associated with a single observable from the viewpoint of skew information. By relaxing ordinary additivity while retaining the other fundamental uncertainty requirements, we introduce a class of Hiai--Petz nonadditive skew informations that contains Hansen's metric-adjusted skew informations as the boundary case [MATH]. Our main quantitative result is a sharp single-observable uncertainty relation for the full Hiai--Petz class. For a fixed state, the optimal coefficient depends only on its largest and smallest eigenvalues and remains sharp even after the maximal classical contribution to the variance is retained. The general theorem yields, as special cases, sharp bounds for metric-adjusted skew informations, the SLD quantum Fisher information, and the power-commutator family. We further show that [MATH], [MATH], is realized within the Hiai--Petz framework through Stolarsky operator means, thereby establishing its convexity for [MATH]. More generally, for each fixed operator monotone function [MATH], the Hiai--Petz spectral kernel interpolates geometrically between the metric-adjusted skew information [MATH] and the common endpoint [MATH]. The resulting family obeys an exact power-trace-weighted composition law, replacing ordinary additivity in the interior [MATH].
tldr: The paper introduces Hiai--Petz nonadditive skew informations and proves a sharp single-observable uncertainty relation for the full class, with applications to metric-adjusted skew information and quantum Fisher information.
motivation: Uncertainty relations for a single observable and skew information are fundamental in quantum information, but existing frameworks are limited by additivity assumptions.
method: By relaxing additivity while retaining the other fundamental uncertainty requirements, the authors define Hiai--Petz nonadditive skew informations and derive optimal state-dependent bounds using Stolarsky operator means and spectral kernel interpolation.
result: The optimal coefficient depends only on the state's largest and smallest eigenvalues, remains sharp even after retaining the maximal classical variance contribution, and covers metric-adjusted skew information, SLD quantum Fisher information, and the power-commutator family.
conclusion: The Hiai--Petz framework yields a convex family obeying an exact power-trace-weighted composition law, replacing ordinary additivity in the interior.

title: Noise-resilient Sequential Circuits For Generating Quantum Order
authors: Konstantin Gattinger, Julian Boesl, Max Mcginley, Michael Knap, Frank Pollmann
abstract: ArXiv:2609.13383v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sequential circuits provide an optimal linear-depth route to unitarily preparing long-range ordered quantum states, but circuit-level noise can be far more damaging than noise applied after preparation: local errors may be propagated by subsequent gates into nonlocal defects that destroy the target order. In this work, we present classes of unitary sequential circuits that prepare certain non-trivial orders in the presence of Pauli noise. Our constructions exploit the spatial structure of the syndromes of the target state, which in certain cases allows us to systematically suppress the propagation of errors using strictly local gates. The strategy can be applied both to symmetry-breaking order, for which we present a 3D example, and to topological order, which we showcase on a 4D version of the toric code. We also highlight how this stability against errors necessitates non-Clifford gates, and how measurement-feedback loops can be used to stabilize lower-dimensional states as well.
tldr: The paper introduces unitary sequential circuits that prepare symmetry-breaking and topological order while resisting circuit-level Pauli noise by exploiting syndrome spatial structure and local gates.
motivation: Sequential circuits provide an optimal linear-depth route to preparing long-range ordered quantum states, but circuit-level noise can propagate local errors into nonlocal defects that destroy the target order, motivating noise-resilient circuit constructions.
method: The authors design classes of unitary sequential circuits for 3D symmetry-breaking order and a 4D toric code, using strictly local gates to suppress error propagation, and they analyze the role of non-Clifford gates and measurement-feedback loops for stabilizing lower-dimensional states.
result: Certain non-trivial orders can be prepared under Pauli noise with error propagation systematically suppressed in some cases, while stability against errors necessitates non-Clifford gates and measurement-feedback can stabilize lower-dimensional states.
conclusion: Noise-resilient sequential circuits offer a promising route to generating quantum order with local control, though robust preparation of lower-dimensional states requires non-Clifford resources and feedback mechanisms.

title: Reservoir Support Sets The Minimum Loss For Non-Hermitian Dynamics
authors: Alena Mastiukova
abstract: ArXiv:2609.13496v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The minimum loss required to reproduce non-Hermitian dynamics depends on how many physical modes each reservoir can address coherently. Established positive-matrix criteria bound this cost. We construct a phase-controlled cubic-root Su-Schrieffer-Heeger chain in which three-mode reservoirs attain the unrestricted passivity threshold throughout its phase diagram and halve the minimum pair-supported loss at a tuned point. The bound constrains exact conditional trajectories, including time-dependent Markov controls, rather than preparation of one final state. A connected-chain protocol tests effective reservoir support through calibrated finite-time emission. Full system-auxiliary propagation then bounds conditional fidelity and target yield for every one-particle input. A coherent controller that accurately prepares the selected endpoint fails this propagator test. A singular-value bound excludes every unitary realization of the same conditional map. These results connect local reservoir access to a measurable loss cost for prescribed dynamics.
tldr: The paper shows that the minimum loss needed to simulate non-Hermitian dynamics is set by the coherent mode support of the reservoir, with a cubic-root SSH chain achieving the unrestricted passivity threshold and halving pair-supported loss.
motivation: Non-Hermitian dynamics arise in open quantum systems, but their physical simulation requires a thermodynamic cost; understanding how reservoir structure bounds this cost is important for controlled quantum dynamics.
method: They construct a phase-controlled cubic-root Su-Schrieffer-Heeger chain and use positive-matrix criteria, system-auxiliary propagation, and singular-value bounds to relate reservoir support to minimum loss and conditional trajectory fidelity.
result: Three-mode reservoirs reach the unrestricted passivity threshold across the phase diagram and halve the minimum pair-supported loss at a tuned point; a coherent controller that prepares the endpoint fails the propagator test, and a singular-value bound excludes any unitary realization of the conditional map.
conclusion: The work connects local reservoir access to a measurable loss cost for prescribed non-Hermitian dynamics and identifies coherent mode support as the key thermodynamic resource.

title: Room-Temperature Storage Of Entanglement In A Silicon Carbide Quantum Node
authors: Shuo Ren, Rui-Jian Liang, Qi-Cheng Hu, Zhen-Xuan He, Ji-Yang Zhou, Wu-Xi Lin, Zhi-He Hao, Tao Tu, Jin-Shi Xu, Chuan-Feng Li, Guang-Can Guo
abstract: ArXiv:2609.13744v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Robust entanglement at room temperature is a central challenge for solid-state quantum information processing and quantum-enhanced sensing. Here we demonstrate room-temperature storage of entanglement in a silicon carbide (SiC) quantum node by coherently transferring an electron-nuclear entangled state onto long-lived nuclear-spin memory qubits. Using a shallow single color center in 4H-SiC, conventionally denoted PL6, we realize a fully addressable three-qubit register composed of one electron-spin processor and two strongly coupled [MATH]Si nuclear-spin memory qubits. This platform enables the deterministic generation of high-fidelity entangled states, including a nuclear-spin Bell state with a fidelity of [MATH] and a three-qubit Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ)-type state with a fidelity of [MATH]. By implementing a SWAP-gate protocol in the strong hyperfine-coupling regime, the electron-nuclear entanglement is transferred to the nuclear-spin memory with a fidelity of [MATH], extending the entanglement lifetime by a factor of 240. We further confirm the generality of this approach in an additional heterogeneous [MATH]Si-[MATH]C nuclear-spin register and, through a statistical survey of 200 single PL6 centers, show that multi-nuclear-spin registers occur naturally with probabilities above 10%. These results position shallow SiC color centers as a powerful platform for entanglement-assisted quantum sensing and scalable room-temperature quantum technologies.
tldr: Room-temperature storage of entanglement is demonstrated in a silicon carbide quantum node by transferring an electron-nuclear entangled state to nuclear-spin memory qubits.
motivation: Robust entanglement at room temperature is a central challenge for solid-state quantum information processing and quantum-enhanced sensing, and SiC color centers offer a promising platform.
method: Using a shallow single PL6 color center in 4H-SiC, a fully addressable three-qubit register is realized with one electron-spin processor and two strongly coupled 29Si nuclear-spin memory qubits; a SWAP-gate protocol in the strong hyperfine-coupling regime transfers electron-nuclear entanglement to the nuclear spins.
result: High-fidelity nuclear-spin Bell and GHZ-type states are generated, entanglement lifetime is extended by a factor of 240, and a statistical survey of 200 PL6 centers shows multi-nuclear-spin registers occur with probabilities above 10%.
conclusion: Shallow SiC color centers are positioned as a powerful platform for entanglement-assisted quantum sensing and scalable room-temperature quantum technologies.

title: Faithful Certification Of Steering- And Incompatibility-breaking Channels
authors: Shin-Liang Chen Po-Ting Hsu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.13885v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider a quantum steering scenario where Alice prepares a bipartite state, sends one subsystem to Bob through a quantum channel, and aims to convince him that their shared state is entangled. Bob, however, will never be convinced if the channel is steering-breaking, that is, if the channel destroys steerability for any input state. To verify that a channel renders a state useless for demonstrating steering, one must consider all possible measurements performed by Alice and check if the conditional states Bob receives admit a local-hidden-state (LHS) model. This is generally a hard problem since it requires considering an infinite number of measurement combinations. Here, we show that the method proposed in [Phys. Rev. Lett. 117, 190401 (2016); Phys. Rev. Lett. 117, 190402 (2016)] can be utilized to tackle this problem. Furthermore, owing to the intimate relation between steering and measurement incompatibility, our approach can faithfully certify whether a channel destroys incompatibility for any set of measurements. Finally, we propose an experimental criterion for certifying steering- and incompatibility-breaking channels, which may be of independent interest.
tldr: The paper shows how to faithfully certify whether a quantum channel destroys steering or measurement incompatibility by reducing the task to checking local-hidden-state models over all Alice measurements.
motivation: Certifying steering-breaking channels is generally hard because it requires considering infinitely many possible measurements by Alice to verify that Bob's conditional states admit an LHS model.
method: The authors adapt a known method from PRL 117, 190401 and 190402 to test LHS models, exploiting the intimate connection between steering and measurement incompatibility.
result: They obtain a faithful certification of steering-breaking and incompatibility-breaking channels and propose an experimental criterion for detecting such channels.
conclusion: The approach provides a practical and faithful way to certify channels that destroy steering or incompatibility, with potential experimental relevance.

title: Broadband Purcell Filter For Fast Superconducting Qubit Reset And Readout
authors: Yu Zhao, Zhixu Chen, Hanxian Liu, Mingze Liu, Zixing Liu, Hao Pang, Meiyan Wan, Changkun Wu, Liuzhu Zhong, Sai Li, Yuefeng Yuan, Yuxuan Zhou, Ji Jiang, Ji Chu, Song Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.14081v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rapid reset and readout of qubit states are essential for quantum error correction, yet accelerating these operations through stronger coupling to a dissipative environment inevitably increases qubit decay via the Purcell effect. Here we present a broadband Purcell filter that decouples the reset and readout paths, enabling both operations to be independently optimized without compromising qubit coherence. The filter employs two engineered notches - an intrinsic notch and a bandstop notch - to provide broadband Purcell protection, together with an additional reset stub that creates a reset mode below the protected band. To enable fast reset while suppressing filter-mediated interactions between qubits, we couple each qubit to a dedicated reset resonator. We experimentally demonstrate Purcell-limited relaxation times exceeding 1 ms across a 1.2 GHz bandwidth, simultaneously with 500 ns readout without a Josephson parametric amplifier and 100 ns reset with 99.6% efficiency. The reset resonator is designed with a deliberate kappa-chi mismatch, which suppresses photon-shot-noise-induced dephasing by a factor of 70 compared to the readout resonator. Our work provides a scalable hardware solution that resolves the traditional trade-off between fast qubit operations and qubit protection, advancing the prospects for fault-tolerant quantum computing.
tldr: A broadband Purcell filter with engineered notches and dedicated reset resonators enables fast superconducting qubit reset and readout while preserving long coherence.
motivation: Fast qubit reset and readout are essential for quantum error correction, but stronger coupling to the environment typically increases qubit decay via the Purcell effect.
method: The authors design a broadband Purcell filter with an intrinsic notch, a bandstop notch, and a reset stub, and couple each qubit to a dedicated reset resonator with a deliberate kappa-chi mismatch.
result: They demonstrate Purcell-limited relaxation times exceeding 1 ms over a 1.2 GHz bandwidth, 500 ns readout without a Josephson parametric amplifier, 100 ns reset with 99.6% efficiency, and 70x suppression of photon-shot-noise-induced dephasing.
conclusion: This scalable hardware solution resolves the trade-off between fast qubit operations and qubit protection, advancing prospects for fault-tolerant quantum computing.

title: Reusable Selected-time Channels For Quantum Simulation Of non-Markovian Dynamics
authors: Yusui Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2609.13456v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Non-Markovian quantum-state diffusion (QSD) provides a microscopic trajectory description of open-system dynamics, but trajectories associated with a chosen initial state are not directly reusable as quantum channels. We develop a constructive framework that converts the QSD propagator into an input-independent Kraus channel for a fixed bath preparation and a selected evolution time. The construction incorporates reservoir memory through a finite-mode approximation of the bath covariance and yields a deterministic channel representation that can be compressed for approximate implementation with a system-ancilla circuit. For the qubit systems considered here, the construction closes exactly in vacuum and extends systematically to finite temperatures. Two-qubit examples with structured reservoirs validate the vacuum channel construction, illustrate its finite-temperature extension for a chosen initial state, and show that the complexity of the reservoir description can differ substantially from the ancilla space required for quantum realization. The framework therefore establishes a direct bridge from microscopic reservoir memory to reusable non-Markovian quantum simulation and provides a foundation for optimized hardware implementations and extensions to larger systems and multitime dynamics.
tldr: The paper develops a constructive framework that converts non-Markovian quantum-state diffusion propagators into reusable selected-time Kraus channels for quantum simulation.
motivation: Non-Markovian QSD trajectories depend on the initial state and are not directly reusable as quantum channels, limiting their use in modular quantum simulation.
method: It approximates the bath covariance with a finite number of modes and constructs an input-independent deterministic channel, compressible for implementation with a system-ancilla circuit.
result: The construction closes exactly for vacuum baths and extends systematically to finite temperatures, with two-qubit structured-reservoir examples validating the approach.
conclusion: The framework bridges microscopic reservoir memory and reusable non-Markovian quantum simulation, providing a foundation for optimized hardware implementations and extensions.

title: Wiser: Systematic Design-Space Exploration Of Fault-Tolerant Global Control Trapped-Ions
authors: Scott Jones, Song-Qing-Hao Yang, Prakash Murali
abstract: ArXiv:2609.13546v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Trapped-ion quantum computers are a leading candidate for scalable fault-tolerant quantum computing, but conventional Quantum Charge-Coupled Device (QCCD) architectures face severe wiring and power constraints as systems scale. The recently proposed WISE promise orders-of-magnitude reductions in wiring complexity but fundamentally alter the hardware--software interface, making it unclear whether such restrictive architectures can feasibly execute quantum error correction (QEC) and eventually support fault-tolerant workloads. We present WISER, a cross-layer architectural design-space exploration framework for globally controlled trapped-ion systems, to determine whether WISE can support early FTQC, and what hardware/compiler/QEC choices are needed. WISER combines novel WISE-specific compilation, noise modelling, and simulation and integrated them into a unified framework. WISER provides comparative lower-bound estimates of logical clock speed and logical error rate, rather than absolute hardware prediction, enabling us to identify viable operating regions while ruling out infeasible ones. To our knowledge, it is the first systematic design space exploration study targeted at WISE and scalable architectures beyond QCCD. title: Identifiability In Quantum State, Process, And Network Tomography
authors: Athira Kalavampara Raghunadhan, Matheus Guedes de Andrade, Don Towsley, Indrakshi Dey, Daniel Kilper, Nicola Marchetti
abstract: ArXiv:2609.13584v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum State Tomography (QST), Quantum Process Tomography (QPT), and Quantum Network Tomography (QNT) are related parameter-estimation problems that aim to reconstruct different physical quantities. QST estimates an unknown quantum state, represented by its density matrix, from the measurement outcomes. QPT characterises an unknown quantum channel using known input states and measurements of the corresponding outputs. QNT, in contrast, aims to infer parameters associated with individual links from end-to-end probe measurements collected at accessible monitor nodes. A key distinction among the three tomography problems lies in the conditions required to achieve identifiability, the ability to determine unknown parameters uniquely from the available measurement statistics. In QST and QPT, the experimenter can choose an Informationally Complete (IC) measurement set. QNT limits the reachable measurements to what topology and monitor placement allow, so the admissible probe paths fix the information available about the link parameters. This work studies all three tomography problems through a common Fisher Information Matrix (FIM). We factorise QNT FIM and show that its rank equals the rank of the path-link incidence matrix at every interior parameter value, so local and global identifiability coincide. We then show that QST and QPT attain full rank under IC settings, QNT loses rank when the probe paths leave link parameters indistinguishable, and increasing the number of copies scales the FIM eigenvalues while leaving its rank fixed.
tldr: A unified Fisher Information Matrix analysis shows identifiability conditions for quantum state, process, and network tomography, with QNT rank tied to the path-link incidence matrix.
motivation: Tomography problems differ in measurement constraints, especially quantum network tomography where topology limits available probes, so understanding identifiability is crucial.
method: They formulate all three tomography problems via a common Fisher Information Matrix, factorize the QNT FIM, and relate its rank to the path-link incidence matrix.
result: QST and QPT achieve full rank under informationally complete measurements, while QNT can lose rank when probe paths make link parameters indistinguishable; increasing copies scales eigenvalues but not rank.
conclusion: Identifiability in QNT is fundamentally constrained by network topology and monitor placement, distinguishing it from QST/QPT.

title: Partial Stabilizer Learning Under Fixed Commuting Constraints And The Absence Of A Copy-Rate Discount
authors: Yimin Lu Masahito Hayashi
abstract: ArXiv:2609.13923v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider an unknown pure stabilizer state of \(n\) qudits with a fixed prime local dimension \(p\), together with prescribed commuting Pauli observables. Rather than learning the whole state, the learner must recover only complementary stabilizers that commute with the prescribed observables, together with their eigenvalues. Once the prescribed measurement is performed, this information and the observed outcome determine the corresponding conditional stabilizer state. We compare the number \(k\) of copies available to the learner with the number \(n\) of qudits and refer to their ratio \(k/n\) as the copy rate. Suppose that the dimension \(m\) of the requested complementary stabilizer subspace satisfies \(m=\beta n+o(n)\) for a fixed \(0<\beta\leq1\). If the copy rate converges to a value below one, the optimal exact recovery probabilities and verification scores converge to zero, both in the worst case and under the uniform prior. Conversely, if the number \(k\) of copies minus the number \(n\) of qudits tends to positive infinity, the entire stabilizer state can be identified with probability tending to one, and the requested complementary information can then be extracted. Thus, restricting the learning target to the stabilizer information needed after the prescribed measurement yields no copy-rate discount.
tldr: The paper studies how many copies of an unknown stabilizer state are needed to recover only the complementary stabilizer information after a prescribed commuting Pauli measurement, showing there is no copy-rate discount for this partial learning task.
motivation: Learning full stabilizer states is a well-studied problem, but practical scenarios may require only partial stabilizer information compatible with fixed commuting observables. The authors ask whether restricting the learning target reduces the required copy rate.
method: They consider an unknown pure stabilizer state of n qudits with fixed prime local dimension p, prescribed commuting Pauli observables, and a target complementary stabilizer subspace of dimension m = βn + o(n). They analyze exact recovery and verification probabilities as functions of the copy rate k/n.
result: If the copy rate converges to a value below one, optimal exact recovery probabilities and verification scores converge to zero in both worst-case and uniform-prior settings. Conversely, if k - n tends to positive infinity, the entire stabilizer state can be identified with probability tending to one, allowing extraction of the requested complementary information.
conclusion: Restricting the learning target to the stabilizer information needed after a prescribed measurement yields no copy-rate discount; asymptotically, nearly full-state learning resources are still required.

title: Quantum Stochastic Walks On The Permutation Group
authors: Feng He, Arthur Hutsalyuk, Giuseppe Mussardo, Andrea Stampiggi
abstract: ArXiv:2609.13387v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How rapidly does order give way to randomness, and can quantum coherence accelerate this process? We address these questions through the paradigmatic problem of card shuffling, formulated as a random walk on the symmetric group [MATH]. We first recast the random-transposition walk studied by Diaconis and Shahshahani, as well as more general walks generated by conjugacy classes of [MATH], in continuous time. We then identify the transition matrix of each classical walk with a permutation Hamiltonian generating a corresponding unitary quantum walk. Purely unitary evolution, however, does not generically converge to the uniform distribution in the classical sense of mixing: coherence preserves information rather than erasing it. We therefore embed the problem into a quantum stochastic walk, where coherent dynamics competes with the dissipative process responsible for classical mixing. In this setting, quantum coherence assists randomization. We prove that it can only decrease the distance from the uniform distribution in the computational basis and can therefore accelerate mixing. An analysis of the slowest mode yields a criterion for the coupling strength required to produce an appreciable speedup. Finally, numerical results reveal a scaling collapse of the ratio between quantum and classical mixing times onto a simple one-parameter form. Our results illustrate how coherence and dissipation can cooperate in the emergence of randomness in walks on permutation groups.
tldr: The paper studies quantum stochastic walks on the symmetric group and shows that quantum coherence can accelerate mixing relative to classical random-transposition walks.
motivation: Card shuffling as a random walk on the symmetric group provides a paradigmatic setting to ask how order gives way to randomness and whether quantum coherence can speed up this process.
method: The authors recast classical walks generated by conjugacy classes as permutation Hamiltonians, embed them into a quantum stochastic walk with competing coherent and dissipative dynamics, and analyze the spectral gap and slowest mode.
result: They prove that coherence cannot increase the distance from the uniform distribution in the computational basis and can accelerate mixing, derive a criterion for the coupling strength needed for appreciable speedup, and numerically observe a scaling collapse of quantum-to-classical mixing-time ratios.
conclusion: The work illustrates how coherence and dissipation can cooperate to produce randomness in walks on permutation groups, connecting quantum stochastic dynamics to mixing phenomena.

title: Braid Map Definition Of SLH-networks And The Series Product
authors: Luc Bouten
abstract: ArXiv:2609.13600v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This article investigates a cascade of quantum systems within an SLH-network. The SLH-network is defined rigorously by using the so-called braid-map. An expression is derived for the time-evolution of the network with finite delay. The series product is retrieved in the instantaneous feed-forward limit.

method: The author uses a braid map to define the network composition, derives the time evolution with finite delay, and takes the instantaneous limit to recover the series product.
