title: Noise-aware Derivative Feedback Of A Harmonic Oscillator Under Quantum-limited Position Measurement
authors: Vedran Vujnovi\'c
abstract: ArXiv:2609.13988v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study measurement-based feedback control of a damped harmonic oscillator, motivated by optomechanical and interferometric position measurements, in which feedback is synthesized from a displacement measurement. For a band-limited derivative controller, the loop shapes the mechanical susceptibility and reinjects measurement noise, creating a tradeoff between stabilization and noise amplification. We present a compact classical formulation that isolates this tradeoff in the closed-loop displacement spectrum and identifies the parameters governing resonance suppression versus noise-driven actuation. We then extend the same topology to a quantum-limited position detector, enforcing the imprecision-backaction constraint and introducing finite measurement bandwidth that regularizes high-frequency noise reinjection and adds phase lag in the feedback path. In the high-[MATH] regime we obtain an analytic design rule for the optimal feedback gain at fixed controller and measurement bandwidths and compare it with full-spectrum calculations. The comparison shows that a high mechanical quality factor alone does not guarantee quantitative agreement: the accuracy of the near-resonant approximation depends strongly on the controller and measurement bandwidths. Because finite measurement bandwidth changes both the magnitude and phase of the feedback loop, the analysis separates the near-resonant damping contribution from imprecision-noise reinjection and shows that positive near-resonant feedback damping requires the product of the controller cutoff and measurement bandwidth to exceed the square of the mechanical resonance frequency. Finally, we present a dimensionless map of the gain-optimized high-[MATH] occupation and compare its predictions with full-spectrum optimization. All analytical gains evaluated in this map satisfy the full closed-loop stability criterion for these parameters.
tldr: The paper analyzes measurement-based derivative feedback control of a damped harmonic oscillator under classical and quantum-limited position detection, deriving design rules for optimal gain and noise tradeoffs.
motivation: Feedback control of harmonic oscillators is central to optomechanical and interferometric position measurements, where quantum-limited detection introduces imprecision-backaction constraints and noise reinjection that must be managed.
method: The author formulates a compact classical closed-loop model for band-limited derivative feedback, then extends it to a quantum-limited position detector by enforcing the imprecision-backaction relation and including finite measurement bandwidth.
result: In the high-Q regime, an analytic design rule for optimal feedback gain is obtained, and positive near-resonant feedback damping requires the product of controller cutoff and measurement bandwidth to exceed the square of the mechanical resonance frequency; high mechanical Q alone does not guarantee quantitative agreement with full-spectrum calculations.
conclusion: A dimensionless map of gain-optimized high-Q occupation is presented, and all analytical gains satisfy the full closed-loop stability criterion for the studied parameters.

title: Shot-based Variational Simulation Of The Toric Code Phase Transition: Energy, Global Entanglement, And Noise Resilience
authors: Mohammad Hossein Zarei Hayede Zarei
abstract: ArXiv:2609.13748v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the capability of variational quantum circuits in detecting a topological phase transition within the toric code model subjected to a uniform magnetic field. The detection is carried out via shot-based computations of both the ground state energy and the global entanglement. We begin by employing well-established renormalization techniques to construct a quantum circuit that accurately represents the pure toric code under periodic boundary condition. This circuit is subsequently parameterized to enable a shot-based variational simulation of the ground state in the presence of the magnetic field. Our results demonstrate that even for the minimal lattice sizes and a finite number of measurement shots, the ground state energy exhibits a distinct singularity at the transition point which can be reliably approximated through finite-size scaling analysis. Furthermore, we introduce a secondary variational circuit designed to compute the global entanglement of the generated ground state. We observe that both global entanglement and its conditional counterpart display the expected qualitative behavior at the transition point, consistent with the topological nature of the phase transition. To evaluate the practical viability of our variational approach on real quantum hardware, we systematically examine the detrimental effects of gate noise on the analysis. We find that the topological phase exhibits a notable robustness against noise, manifesting as a linear decrease in the transition point with increasing noise strength.
tldr: The paper uses shot-based variational quantum circuits to detect the topological phase transition of the toric code under a magnetic field, tracking ground-state energy and global entanglement while characterizing noise resilience.
motivation: The toric code is a paradigmatic topological error-correcting model, and understanding whether near-term variational quantum algorithms can reliably probe its field-induced phase transition is of practical interest for near-term quantum devices.
method: A renormalization-inspired circuit for the pure toric code under periodic boundary conditions is parameterized and optimized shot-by-shot to approximate the ground state in a magnetic field, with a secondary variational circuit computing global entanglement and its conditional variant, plus a systematic study of gate noise.
result: The ground-state energy shows a clear singularity at the transition for minimal lattices and finite shots, approximable via finite-size scaling; global entanglement displays the expected behavior at the transition, and the transition point decreases linearly with noise strength, indicating robustness of the topological phase.
conclusion: Shot-based variational simulation can qualitatively capture the toric code phase transition and its entanglement signature, and the topological phase exhibits notable noise resilience, though the approach remains limited to small lattices and qualitative agreement.

title: Cuda-q Logical: Retargetable Compilation For Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing
authors: Alexander Mccaskey, Justin Lietz, Adam Holmes, Kohei Nakaji, Vadym Kliuchnikov, Yifan Hong, Amalee Wilson, Andres Paz, Bettina Heim, Bruno Schmitt, Krysta M. Svore
abstract: ArXiv:2609.13388v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Realizing fault-tolerant quantum computing requires mapping logical programs to heterogeneous quantum error correction (QEC) codes and diverse fault-tolerant execution models, scheduling physical resources, and coupling to real-time classical control and feedback. Specialized tools exist for each step but rely on manual composition and translation that discard assumptions and provenance, separating resource estimates from the compiler artifacts they describe, and making it difficult to validate correctness, compare architectures, or attribute costs to specific design choices. We present CUDA-Q Logical, an extensible compiler infrastructure for retargetable fault-tolerant compilation, analysis, and execution. Interoperable with CUDA-Q and other mainstream front-ends, CUDA-Q Logical progressively lowers target-independent logical programs through a constrained logical virtual machine, QEC microcode, physical gate schedules, and real-time control plans, with each layer preserving semantics and provenance, while verifying composition and resource constraints. By deriving every resource estimate directly from compiler artifacts, the framework unifies compilation and resource analysis, enabling successively refined estimates and principled cross-architecture comparison while permitting QEC codes, execution models, decoders, and hardware architectures to be introduced as modular extensions. Across workloads ranging from application-architecture studies to qLDPC surgery and detector-error-model composition, we show that schedule-derived estimates reconcile with established independent models. Crucially, this compiler-visible structure exposes cost drivers hidden by aggregate analytical formulas, carries QEC artifacts intact into simulation, and demonstrates a complete compilation pipeline for fault-tolerant quantum computing.
tldr: CUDA-Q Logical is an extensible compiler infrastructure that lowers target-independent logical quantum programs through a constrained logical VM, QEC microcode, physical gate schedules, and real-time control plans while preserving semantics and provenance.
motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires mapping logical programs onto heterogeneous QEC codes and diverse execution models, but existing specialized tools are manually composed, discard provenance, and disconnect resource estimates from the compiler artifacts they describe, hindering validation and cross-architecture comparison.
method: The framework progressively lowers programs through layered representations (logical VM, QEC microcode, physical schedules, real-time control), verifying composition and resource constraints at each layer and deriving all resource estimates directly from compiler artifacts, with QEC codes, decoders, execution models, and hardware as modular extensions.
result: Across workloads spanning application-architecture studies, qLDPC surgery, and detector-error-model composition, schedule-derived resource estimates reconcile with established independent analytical models while exposing cost drivers hidden by aggregate formulas.
conclusion: The work demonstrates a complete compilation pipeline for fault-tolerant quantum computing, unifying compilation and resource analysis and enabling principled cross-architecture comparison through a retargetable, provenance-preserving infrastructure.

title: Time Domain Non-linear Quantum Interferometry
authors: C. Fruy, A. Th\'ery, B. Hue, W. Legrand, L. Jarjat, J. Craquelin, M. R. Delbecq, A. Cottet, T. Kontos
abstract: ArXiv:2609.13749v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Interferometry is a powerful method for studying many fundamental phenomena ranging from gravitational waves to anyon excitations. Besides loss of coherence in the interferometer paths, quantum mechanics sets an incompressible bound for linear interferometry arising from the quantum noise of the light beam, called the shot noise limit. Here, we implement a non-linear quantum interferometer that uses a microwave cavity and a magnetic field resilient anharmonic superconducting quantum circuit made of granular aluminum. The circuit enables interferometry beyond the shot noise limit. A direct application of our findings is the detection of dark matter (axions or dark photons), high-frequency gravitational waves or astronomical masers.
tldr: A time-domain nonlinear quantum interferometer using a microwave cavity and a granular-aluminum superconducting circuit achieves interferometry beyond the shot noise limit, targeting dark matter and gravitational wave detection.
motivation: Linear interferometry is fundamentally limited by shot noise from quantum fluctuations, so nonlinear quantum interferometry is sought to surpass this bound for detecting extremely weak signals.
method: The authors implement a nonlinear quantum interferometer by coupling a microwave cavity to a magnetic-field-resilient anharmonic superconducting circuit made of granular aluminum.
result: The circuit enables interferometry beyond the shot noise limit, with direct applications to detecting dark matter candidates such as axions or dark photons, high-frequency gravitational waves, and astronomical masers.
conclusion: Nonlinear quantum interferometry with superconducting circuits offers a promising route to enhanced sensitivity for fundamental physics searches, though it is primarily a sensing/metrology application rather than a quantum information or thermodynamic result.

title: Orientation-dependent Pauli Noise In One-dimensional Discrete-time Quantum Walks
authors: Alejandro Contreras Reynoso, Adrian Ortega, Thomas Gorin
abstract: ArXiv:2609.13392v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Discrete-time quantum walks exhibit ballistic spreading that is highly sensitive to decoherence. We study the long-time dynamics of a one-dimensional discrete-time quantum walk under Pauli noise acting on the coin. Choosing the unitary coin such that its invariant Bloch-sphere axis is orthogonal to the axis fixed by the conditional shift, we identify the distinct effects of noise aligned with either dynamical axis or orthogonal to both. Using a Fourier-space Pauli-superoperator formalism, we derive expressions for the first two position moments and long-time asymptotics for X-, Y-, Z-, and depolarizing noise. All channels induce a crossover from ballistic to diffusive spreading, with a second moment growing linearly at long times. The approach to this regime is channel dependent: it is exponentially fast for X-, Z-, and depolarizing noise, but algebraic, with a leading [MATH] correction, for Y-noise. The position distributions retain distinct finite-noise signatures, including a Gaussian-like profile with a central depression for Y-noise. In the maximal-noise limit, depolarizing, Y-, and Z-noise yield the classical binomial distribution for arbitrary initial coin states, whereas X-noise does so only when the initial state has no component along the noise axis. Thus, the quantum-to-classical transition is governed by the relative alignment of the noise, the coherent walk dynamics, and the initial state.
tldr: The paper analyzes how Pauli noise on the coin of a one-dimensional discrete-time quantum walk induces a crossover from ballistic to diffusive spreading, with channel- and orientation-dependent signatures.
motivation: Discrete-time quantum walks are highly sensitive to decoherence, but the role of noise orientation relative to the walk's dynamical axes is not fully understood.
method: Using a Fourier-space Pauli-superoperator formalism, the authors derive the first two position moments and long-time asymptotics for X-, Y-, Z-, and depolarizing noise on the coin.
result: All channels lead to diffusive spreading at long times, but the approach to this regime is exponential for X-, Z-, and depolarizing noise while algebraic for Y-noise; position distributions show distinct finite-noise signatures, including a central depression for Y-noise.
conclusion: The quantum-to-classical transition depends on the relative alignment of the noise, the coherent walk dynamics, and the initial coin state; in the maximal-noise limit, depolarizing, Y-, and Z-noise yield the classical binomial distribution for arbitrary initial coin states, whereas X-noise does so only when the initial state has no component along the noise axis.

title: Thermodynamic Geometry Of Inclusion Statistics
authors: M. H. Naghizadeh Ardabili, Omid Yahyayi Monem, Habib Esmaili, Zahra Ebadi, Hosein Mohammadzadeh
abstract: ArXiv:2609.13787v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the thermodynamic geometry of an ideal quantum gas obeying inclusion statistics, characterized by a negative statistical parameter [MATH]. In this framework the grand-canonical partition function admits a finite maximum fugacity, and the thermodynamic scalar curvature [MATH] is strictly positive for all [MATH], reflecting effective attractive statistical interactions analogous to those of a bosonic system. As the fugacity approaches its maximum value, [MATH] diverges, signaling a phase transition of the Bose-Einstein condensation type. A key distinction from the ordinary ideal Bose gas is that the condensation temperature is elevated relative to the bosonic case, and finite-temperature condensation occurs even in the dimensional regime [MATH] where standard bosons do not condense, while for [MATH] the transition temperature vanishes. Three independent criteria; divergence of [MATH], the maximum fugacity singularity, and the non-analytic cusp in the specific heat, coincide at the same condensation point, confirming the thermodynamic consistency of the transition.
tldr: The paper investigates the thermodynamic geometry of an ideal quantum gas obeying inclusion statistics, revealing a positive scalar curvature and a Bose-Einstein-like condensation at elevated temperature.
motivation: To explore how generalized quantum statistics with a negative statistical parameter affect thermodynamic geometry and condensation phenomena.
method: The authors compute the grand-canonical partition function, thermodynamic scalar curvature, and analyze three independent criteria for condensation in inclusion statistics.
result: The scalar curvature is strictly positive and diverges as fugacity approaches its maximum; condensation occurs at a higher temperature than for bosons, even in two dimensions, with all criteria coinciding at the transition point.
conclusion: Inclusion statistics yields a thermodynamically consistent description with distinctive condensation features, including condensation in 2D and a vanishing transition temperature in 1D.

title: Torsion Detection In Clique Complexes Is Conditionally $QMA_1$-hard
authors: Adam Weso{\l}owski
abstract: ArXiv:2609.14110v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum algorithms for topological data analysis compute Betti numbers, the ranks of the homology groups of a simplicial complex, which can be read off from the kernel of a combinatorial Laplacian. Deciding whether a Betti number of a clique complex is nonzero is [MATH]-hard, and remains so under a spectral gap promise on vertex-weighted graphs. Integral homology, however, contains information inaccessible to the Laplacian spectrum. A new part that appears in integral homology is torsion: cycles that become boundaries only after being traversed several times, as in a projective plane or a Klein bottle. We ask how hard it is to detect torsion, and we answer with a simple reduction. We attach to an arbitrary clique complex a fixed [MATH]-vertex triangulation of the projective plane. The [MATH]th mod-[MATH] Betti number of the input then reappears as [MATH]-torsion two degrees up, while all rational homology disappears and every combinatorial Laplacian acquires a constant spectral gap. We conclude that detecting torsion in clique complexes of unweighted graphs is [MATH]-hard, even under a constant gap promise, and that it is [MATH]-hard if mod-[MATH] clique homology is.
tldr: The paper proves that detecting torsion in clique complexes of unweighted graphs is conditionally QMA1-hard, even under a constant spectral gap promise.
motivation: Integral homology contains torsion information that is invisible to the Laplacian spectrum, and the computational hardness of detecting such torsion in quantum topological data analysis was previously unclear.
method: A fixed triangulation of the projective plane is attached to an arbitrary clique complex, turning the mod-2 Betti number of the input into 2-torsion two degrees higher, while killing rational homology and ensuring all combinatorial Laplacians have a constant spectral gap.
result: Torsion detection in clique complexes is QMA1-hard under a constant gap promise, and QMA-hard if mod-2 clique homology is QMA-hard.
conclusion: This establishes conditional quantum hardness for torsion detection, showing that topological data analysis beyond Betti numbers is computationally intractable under standard complexity assumptions.

title: Adaptive Coding For Two-Way Wiretap Channels With One-Sided Strong Secrecy
authors: Yanling Chen Masahito Hayashi
abstract: ArXiv:2609.13832v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a discrete memoryless two-way wiretap channel under strong one-sided secrecy, where User 1's message is confidential and User 2's message is not required to be secret. We develop non-adaptive and key-assisted adaptive inner bounds from a common resolvability estimate for selected index components. For the adaptive construction, we prove a multiround leakage theorem that accounts both for information revealed about a key before its later use and for the possibility that an encoder uses an incorrectly decoded key. The proof includes an ideal-to-implemented coupling, deterministic codebook selection, and a growing-round argument that removes the initialization-rate loss. We eliminate the internal component rates exactly and characterize the adaptive gain at each fixed auxiliary distribution. For an open two-parameter family of binary channels, we also prove a converse for arbitrary non-adaptive stochastic codes and obtain an operational adaptive-versus-non-adaptive separation. For one representative channel, the complete non-adaptive strong one-sided secrecy capacity region is identified exactly.
tldr: The paper develops adaptive coding schemes for two-way wiretap channels with one-sided strong secrecy, providing inner bounds and a converse for a family of binary channels.
motivation: Secure communication over two-way channels where only one user's message needs confidentiality is less understood than one-way settings, especially with strong secrecy and adaptive coding.
method: Information-theoretic achievability via resolvability, a multiround leakage theorem, ideal-to-implemented coupling, and deterministic codebook selection; converse for non-adaptive stochastic codes.
result: Adaptive inner bounds, an operational separation between adaptive and non-adaptive strategies, and exact non-adaptive strong one-sided secrecy capacity region for a representative binary channel.
conclusion: Adaptive coding can improve secrecy rates in two-way wiretap channels, and the gain is characterized at each fixed auxiliary distribution.

title: Digital Quantum Lattice Boltzmann Evolution By Reversible Compute And Open-system Reset
authors: Muhammad Idrees Khan
abstract: ArXiv:2609.13953v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Turbulent fluid simulation is computationally demanding because nonlinear interactions couple a wide range of scales. Quantum computing offers another computational model, but fluid evolution is nonlinear and dissipative whereas closed gate-based dynamics is linear and reversible. The lattice Boltzmann method (LBM) is an attractive discrete target because streaming is a local permutation, yet conventional collision reconstructs a nonlinear equilibrium and applies dissipative relaxation. We present a digital quantum lattice Boltzmann (QLBM) algorithm that keeps that nonlinear timestep in computational-basis registers. Each step writes the updated populations into a clean destination bank, uncomputes the workspace, and resets the obsolete source. The resulting channel is completely positive and trace preserving (CPTP), composes without intermediate measurement, and applies to any lattice Boltzmann stencil that can be evaluated reversibly into a clean bank. Forced D3Q19 homogeneous isotropic turbulence, in direct numerical simulation (DNS) and Smagorinsky large-eddy simulation (LES) at Reynolds number 15000 over one million lattice steps, shows statistical agreement in mass, energy budgets, spectra, and intermittency. The three-dimensional calculations use a digital-register emulator of the circuit. A separate D2Q9 implementation compiles the same contract to reversible gates and agrees bit-exactly with its integer twin. Two-bank storage and serial lattice depth limit near-term feasibility.
tldr: A digital quantum lattice Boltzmann algorithm using reversible computation and open-system reset simulates turbulent fluid dynamics.
motivation: Turbulent fluid simulation is computationally demanding, and quantum computing offers an alternative, but fluid evolution is nonlinear and dissipative whereas closed gate-based dynamics is linear and reversible.
method: The algorithm keeps the nonlinear lattice Boltzmann timestep in computational-basis registers, writes updated populations into a clean destination bank, uncomputes the workspace, and resets the obsolete source, yielding a CPTP channel that composes without intermediate measurement.
result: Forced D3Q19 homogeneous isotropic turbulence simulations at Reynolds number 15000 over one million steps show statistical agreement with classical DNS/LES, and a D2Q9 implementation compiles to reversible gates with bit-exact agreement.
conclusion: The approach enables digital quantum simulation of fluid dynamics, though near-term feasibility is limited by two-bank storage and serial lattice depth.

title: A New Upper Bound On The Binary Deletion Channel Capacity
authors: \"ozg\"ur Soysal
abstract: ArXiv:2609.13351v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove that the capacity of the binary deletion channel satisfies [MATH] for every [MATH]. The proof describes the output from right to left, using a six-bit context to assign a description length. We bound the increase in expected description length minus output entropy when one input bit is added. A relative-entropy identity reduces this bound to finitely many linear inequalities. A potential on input windows of length 26 makes the inequalities telescope, giving a bound for every input word. Deletion composition extends the result from [MATH] to all larger deletion probabilities. We also obtain finite-block bounds on mutual information and decoding error, with explicit [MATH] corrections. The finite certificate is checked using exact integer arithmetic, and the proof is formalized end to end in Lean.
tldr: The paper proves a new upper bound on the capacity of the binary deletion channel for every deletion probability, with finite-block bounds and a Lean-formalized proof.
motivation: The binary deletion channel is a fundamental model in classical information theory, but its exact capacity remains unknown except in special cases, motivating sharper upper bounds.
method: The proof describes the output from right to left using a six-bit context, bounds the increase in expected description length minus output entropy, reduces the bound to finitely many linear inequalities via a relative-entropy identity, and uses a potential on 26-bit windows to telescope the inequalities; deletion composition extends the result to all deletion probabilities.
result: An upper bound on the binary deletion channel capacity is established for all deletion probabilities, along with finite-block bounds on mutual information and decoding error with explicit corrections, and the finite certificate is checked in exact integer arithmetic and formalized in Lean.
conclusion: This work advances the classical theory of deletion channels by providing a rigorously verified upper bound and finite-block analysis, though it is not directly connected to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Suture: Syndrome-Guided Repair For Segmented Feasibility-Preserving VQAs On Noisy Hardware
authors: Sokea Sang, Leanghok Hour, Sanghyeon Lee, Youngsun Han
abstract: ArXiv:2609.13935v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Constrained binary optimization is a representative class of NP-hard problems in scheduling, resource allocation, and finance. Segmented feasibility-preserving variational quantum algorithms (VQAs) are a promising approach that restricts ideal circuit evolution to feasible assignments and executes short measure-and-reseed segments. The existing boundary runtime enforces feasibility through purification, which discards measurements that violate the constraints. As problem size and noise increase, feasible measurements become rare; if no shot survives, the execution chain terminates. In our 72-qubit graph-coloring experiment on a real-device IBM Heron, 11 of 12 purification chains terminate before completing all segments. We propose SUTURE: syndrome-guided repair, a runtime that repairs infeasible measurements instead of discarding them and is deployable on current quantum devices. SUTURE exploits a parity-check-like structure induced by the problem constraints: violated constraints form a syndrome that detects and localizes corruption and, under suitable structural conditions, often identifies a correction. SUTURE combines three stages: (1) a compile-time profiler that uses the compiled constraints and feasible initialization samples to predict single-flip recovery, with a maximum error of 0.011 across four constraint families; (2) a bounded runtime decoder that replaces purification inside the segmented execution loop; and (3) a regime analysis that identifies when repair is preferable to purification. In simulation up to 120 qubits, SUTURE continues the execution chain far beyond the noise level at which purification collapses. In the same 72-qubit experiment on IBM Heron hardware, SUTURE completes all segments in all 12 runs, and hardware timing experiment, decoding adds 1.6% to execution-path latency and less than 1% to total pipeline latency.
tldr: SUTURE is a syndrome-guided repair runtime for segmented feasibility-preserving VQAs that repairs infeasible measurements instead of discarding them, sustaining execution on noisy hardware.
motivation: Segmented feasibility-preserving VQAs rely on purification to reject infeasible measurements, but as noise and problem size grow, feasible shots become rare and execution chains terminate before completing all segments.
method: SUTURE uses a compile-time profiler to predict single-flip recovery from compiled constraints and feasible samples, a bounded runtime decoder that replaces purification inside the segmented loop, and a regime analysis for choosing repair over purification.
result: In simulations up to 120 qubits, SUTURE continues execution far beyond the noise level where purification collapses; on a 72-qubit IBM Heron experiment, it completes all segments in all 12 runs, adding 1.6% to execution-path latency and under 1% to total pipeline latency.
conclusion: Syndrome-guided repair offers a practical, low-overhead alternative to purification for maintaining feasibility and preserving VQA execution chains on current noisy quantum devices.

title: Structured Quantum Kernels For Chaotic Forecasting
authors: Zhihui Wang, Sujit Roy, Ata Akbari, Manil Maskey, Rahul Ramachandran
abstract: ArXiv:2609.13360v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum kernels promise exponentially large feature spaces, but expressive circuits render their Gram matrices uninformative, bandwidth tuning collapses them toward classical RBF, and the practical consensus is that quantum kernels add nothing on classical data. We answer another productive question, an architectural one: whether the structure of an encoding circuit can carry an inductive bias that tuned classical kernels lack. We introduce AeRot, a quantum kernel fusing amplitude encoding of l2-normalized delay windows with a grouped single-qubit rotation layer that assigns contiguous temporal blocks to each qubit, making the circuit delay-window-aware. On Lorenz-63 kernel ridge regression with cross-validated bandwidths over 100 seeds, AeRot outperforms tuned RBF and Matern-5/2, the advantage emerging at physical horizons >= 0.15 tu and reaching +0.137 mean R^2 at 0.25 tu (5 qubits, window 32). Linear-stability analysis of the window tail localises the advantage to the unstable saddle-approach regime: AeRot wins 83% of windows in the most unstable decile, with the win rate rising monotonically with tail instability and a sign flip at the local stability boundary. The difficulty is fold-branch ambiguity: trajectories approaching the saddle are locally diverging, and Euclidean kernels struggle to resolve which lobe the trajectory will commit to. Structural diagnostics confirm Gram matrices structurally distinct from tuned RBF, with strictly higher target-kernel alignment at every horizon. The gain is architectural: a finite-sample inductive-bias effect of temporally structured encoding on a folded attractor, with no computational-separation claim attached. To our knowledge this is the first mechanistic localisation of quantum-kernel advantage to a specific dynamical regime of a classical system.
tldr: The paper introduces AeRot, a structured quantum kernel whose encoding circuit is made delay-window-aware, and shows a finite-sample inductive-bias advantage over tuned classical kernels specifically for forecasting trajectories approaching the unstable saddle of the Lorenz-63 attractor.
motivation: Quantum kernels are widely believed to add nothing over tuned classical kernels on classical data because expressive circuits give uninformative Gram matrices and bandwidth tuning collapses them to RBF kernels; the authors instead ask whether the architecture of the encoding circuit can supply an inductive bias that tuned classical kernels lack.
method: AeRot fuses amplitude encoding of l2-normalized delay windows with a grouped single-qubit rotation layer assigning contiguous temporal blocks to each qubit, and is evaluated via kernel ridge regression on Lorenz-63 with cross-validated bandwidths across 100 seeds, supplemented by Gram-matrix diagnostics and linear-stability analysis of the window tail.
result: AeRot outperforms tuned RBF and Matérn-5/2 kernels at physical horizons >= 0.15 tu, reaching +0.137 mean R^2 at 0.25 tu (5 qubits, window 32), winning 83% of windows in the most unstable decile with the win rate rising monotonically with tail instability and flipping sign at the local stability boundary.
conclusion: The advantage is architectural—a finite-sample inductive-bias effect of temporally structured encoding on a folded attractor, with no computational-separation claim—and is presented as the first mechanistic localization of a quantum-kernel advantage to a specific dynamical regime of a classical system.

title: Handling Imperfections In Subcircuit Compilation For Linear Optical Quantum Computing
authors: Tobias Forster, Yannick Stade, Andreas Fyrillas, Jean Senellart, Lukas Burgholzer, Robert Wille
abstract: ArXiv:2609.13379v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Linear Optical Quantum Computing (LOQC) is emerging as a promising technology in large-scale quantum computing. Corresponding devices, including linear optical circuits, are rapidly growing in size and fabrication precision. However, even with improved quality, the circuits still exhibit imperfections leading to photon loss or phase noise that vary across the circuit. Already small deficiencies can have a vast impact on both accuracy and efficiency. For computations that do not require the entire linear optical circuit, so-called subcircuits, one can choose where to perform the computation, opening optimization opportunities that are addressed by subcircuit compilation. Current compilers spread the subcircuit's computation across the entire circuit, connecting the same input and output ports, thereby failing to fully exploit the optimization opportunities. However, given the subcircuit's reduced size compared to the entire circuit, one can keep its implementation localized and intentionally route photons to connect good input and output ports. This, however, is a highly non-trivial task, as numerous options must be weighed against one another, and the quality of the solution is influenced by a wide range of hardware parameters. In particular, the reflectivities of imperfect beam splitters can lead to photon losses during routing, which must be traded off against losses at the input and output ports due to imperfect transmission rates. Since current compilers do not account for these effects, we propose the first efficient subcircuit compilation method that optimizes for the coincidence rate, the probability of successfully measuring all desired photons, by handling hardware imperfections. Our evaluations demonstrate significant improvement over existing methods in robustness against phase noise and significantly increased coincidence rates across all benchmarks of up to plus 33.2%.
tldr: The paper proposes the first subcircuit compilation method for linear optical quantum computing that explicitly accounts for hardware imperfections (beam-splitter reflectivity, photon loss, phase noise) to maximize the coincidence rate of localized subcircuit implementations.
motivation: Existing LOQC subcircuit compilers spread computations across the whole linear optical circuit, ignoring that imperfect beam splitters and input/output ports introduce spatially varying photon loss and phase noise, leaving optimization opportunities unexploited.
method: The authors formulate subcircuit compilation as an optimization over localized implementation and photon routing choices, trading off routing losses at imperfect beam splitters against transmission losses at input/output ports, and design an efficient algorithm optimizing the coincidence rate.
result: Evaluations show significant robustness against phase noise and improvements in coincidence rate of up to +33.2% across all benchmarks compared to existing compilers.
conclusion: Incorporating hardware imperfection models into subcircuit compilation substantially improves practical LOQC circuit performance, motivating imperfection-aware compilation strategies for photonic quantum computing.

title: Heuristic Quantum Amplitude Amplification: A Traffic Qubo Case Study
authors: Daniel Koch Kip Nieman
abstract: ArXiv:2609.13505v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum Amplitude Amplification (QAA), the generalization of Grover's algorithm, is well-positioned for combinatorial optimization and is particularly promising for Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) problems. QAA is appealing due to its ability to drive the quantum system to a target state, yielding the globally optimal solution with probability over [MATH]+%. However, realizing QAA for application-scale optimization currently exceeds quantum hardware capacity, which is further compounded by unresolved algorithmic challenges regarding the choice of free parameters. In this study, we address these issues by utilizing a realistic traffic flow QUBO problem to investigate the implementation of QAA as a heuristic solver. Specifically, allowing the diffusion operator parameter to take non-[MATH] values expands the capabilities of QAA. This unlocks a new multiple-shot, low-iteration strategy that aims for a high cumulative probability rather than maximizing the probability of a single basis state. Using [MATH]-qubit simulations, our results demonstrate that heuristic QAA addresses two of the main challenges cited in previous studies. Firstly, heuristic QAA works even at a single iteration, reducing circuit depth by orders of magnitude compared to standard QAA. And secondly, we show that the problem-dependent parameters necessary for reaching optimal algorithmic performance can be reliably approximated with minimal upfront classical computing overhead.
tldr: A numerical case study showing that heuristic Quantum Amplitude Amplification with a tunable diffusion parameter can heuristically solve a traffic-flow QUBO problem using a multi-shot, low-iteration strategy.
motivation: Realizing standard QAA for application-scale combinatorial optimization exceeds current hardware capacity and suffers from unresolved choices of free parameters, so the authors explore a heuristic relaxation suited to near-term devices.
method: They formulate a realistic traffic flow problem as a QUBO, allow the diffusion operator parameter to take non-standard values, and study a multiple-shot, low-iteration strategy via numerical simulation on a small number of qubits.
result: Heuristic QAA performs well even at a single iteration, reducing circuit depth by orders of magnitude relative to standard QAA, and the problem-dependent parameters needed for good performance can be approximated with minimal classical overhead.
conclusion: Heuristic QAA is proposed as a practical near-term solver for optimization problems, though the work remains an applied algorithmic/simulation study without an information-theoretic contribution.

title: Pqln: Post-Quantum Security For The Bitcoin Lightning Network's Off-Chain Surfaces
authors: Ahmet Kurt, Abdul-Salem Beibitkhan, Yacoub Hanna, Abdullah Aydeger
abstract: ArXiv:2609.13781v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A cryptographically relevant quantum computer will break the elliptic-curve cryptography behind Bitcoin and its Lightning Network, the most widely used payment channel network. Even a post-quantum consensus upgrade of Bitcoin would not cover Lightning's off-chain surfaces, so its gossip, peer transport, invoices, payment onions, and offers need separate protection. An adversary can already record Lightning's encrypted traffic today and decrypt it once such a computer exists. Lightning can therefore move to post-quantum cryptography now, without waiting for Bitcoin, and stop such harvest-now-decrypt-later attacks along with node impersonation, invoice forgery, and payment deanonymization. In this paper, we propose PQLN, a hybrid post-quantum extension of Lightning that protects all of these surfaces with the lattice-based standards ML-DSA and ML-KEM. PQLN distributes post-quantum node identities through Lightning's gossip, hybridizes the transport handshake, adds post-quantum signatures to invoices, commits post-quantum keys in offers, and makes payment onions hybrid. Since post-quantum material is much larger than its elliptic-curve counterpart, we introduce techniques that fit it into Lightning's existing message formats and size limits. We analyze the security of PQLN against a quantum adversary and implement it in rust-lightning, a major Lightning implementation. Our evaluation with real Lightning nodes shows that PQLN nodes interoperate with unmodified nodes. The added cryptographic operations take at most 0.33 milliseconds, and the main cost is communication, since gossip data grows about tenfold with ML-DSA and about fourfold with the smaller Falcon. To our knowledge, PQLN is the first post-quantum design, implementation, and evaluation for Lightning.
tldr: PQLN is a hybrid post-quantum extension of the Bitcoin Lightning Network that protects its off-chain surfaces (gossip, transport, invoices, onions, offers) using ML-DSA and ML-KEM.
motivation: A cryptographically relevant quantum computer would break the elliptic-curve cryptography underpinning Bitcoin's Lightning Network, and even a post-quantum consensus upgrade would leave Lightning's off-chain surfaces exposed to harvest-now-decrypt-later attacks.
method: The authors design PQLN, distributing post-quantum node identities via gossip, hybridizing the transport handshake, adding post-quantum signatures to invoices, committing post-quantum keys in offers, and making payment onions hybrid, while encoding the larger post-quantum material into Lightning's existing message formats and size limits; they implement it in rust-lightning.
result: PQLN nodes interoperate with unmodified Lightning nodes, added cryptographic operations cost at most 0.33 ms, but gossip data grows roughly tenfold with ML-DSA and about fourfold with Falcon, making communication the dominant cost.
conclusion: PQLN is claimed to be the first post-quantum design, implementation, and evaluation for the Lightning Network, offering immediate protection against quantum adversaries without waiting for a Bitcoin consensus upgrade.

title: Energy Is Not Enough: Leakage-Aware Ansatz Criterion For Variational Quantum Eigensolvers
authors: Yuan-Chieh Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2609.13521v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In molecular variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) calculations for a fixed electron-number sector, the projected-sector energy alone does not certify that a prepared state is physically valid. We show that a state can have zero projected-sector error while almost all of its probability mass lies outside the target particle-number sector. We therefore evaluate ansatz families using three quantities: projected-sector error, leakage outside the physical sector and parameter count. Our noiseless experiments show that particle-preserving UCC-style families eliminate leakage induced by ansatze, but do not guarantee ground-state accuracy. In the parameter-budget comparison experiments, the one-shot ranking rules select identical generator sequences and yield identical errors. The adaptive hybrid procedure achieves lower mean projected-sector errors at selected budgets. Using established Kraus invariant-subspace criteria, we also express channel-induced leakage through a positive operator and discuss global and local depolarizing noise analytically. This gives a practical diagnostic framework for comparing ansatze beyond energy alone.
tldr: The paper argues that projected-sector energy alone cannot certify a physically valid VQE state and proposes a leakage-aware ansatz diagnostic using projected-sector error, sector leakage, and parameter count.
motivation: In molecular VQE within a fixed electron-number sector, a state can show zero projected energy error while most of its probability mass lies outside the target particle-number sector, so energy alone is an unreliable validation metric.
method: Ansatz families (particle-preserving UCC-style, one-shot ranking rules, adaptive hybrid procedures) are benchmarked with three metrics — projected-sector error, leakage outside the physical sector, and parameter count — and channel-induced leakage is analyzed via Kraus invariant-subspace criteria for global and local depolarizing noise.
result: Particle-preserving UCC-style ansätze eliminate ansatz-induced leakage but do not guarantee ground-state accuracy; one-shot ranking rules select identical generator sequences with identical errors, while the adaptive hybrid procedure achieves lower mean projected-sector errors at selected budgets.
conclusion: Energy error alone is insufficient for validating VQE preparations, and the proposed leakage-aware diagnostic framework offers a practical way to compare ansätze beyond energy.

title: Symmetric Models For Syndrome Decoding
authors: Simone Trebiani Elisa Gorla
abstract: ArXiv:2609.14052v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper introduces a new polynomial model for the exact variant of the Syndrome Decoding Problem (SDP) in the binary case. The model is based on elementary symmetric polynomials. We estimate the computational complexity of solving the corresponding polynomial system by establishing bounds on the degree of regularity and on the solving degree of the ideal associated to the model. The complexity estimate is lower than for previous polynomial models. We also provide a variant of the model whose complexity depends directly on the specific instance of the SDP and is lower than for the first model. Finally, we discuss how to apply our approach to solve other variants of the SDP.
tldr: Introduces a new polynomial model for the exact binary Syndrome Decoding Problem using elementary symmetric polynomials, with improved complexity bounds for algebraic solving.
motivation: Syndrome decoding underpins code-based post-quantum cryptography, so better algebraic attacks and complexity estimates help assess security margins.
method: The exact SDP is encoded as a polynomial system via elementary symmetric polynomials; the solving degree and degree of regularity are bounded to estimate computational complexity.
result: The new model yields lower complexity estimates than previous polynomial models, and an instance-dependent variant achieves even lower complexity.
conclusion: The approach provides more efficient algebraic modeling for the SDP and can be adapted to other SDP variants, relevant to cryptanalysis of post-quantum schemes.

title: Weight Spectra Of Some Families Of Grm Codes
authors: Minjia Shi, Zhaokang Xing, Patrick Sole
abstract: ArXiv:2609.13653v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let [MATH] denote the generalized Reed--Muller code of order [MATH] and length [MATH] over the finite field [MATH]. We completely determine the weight spectra of [MATH] for [MATH], [MATH] for [MATH], [MATH], and [MATH], in the ranges of [MATH] specified in the corresponding results. The proofs proceed by induction on [MATH], using a sumset inclusion for GRM weight spectra together with results on low-weight codewords. motivation: Weight spectra of Reed-Muller-type codes are a classical, long-standing combinatorial problem in coding theory, important for understanding code structure and low-weight codeword behavior.
method: The proofs use induction on the code order, a sumset inclusion relation for GRM weight spectra, and known results on low-weight codewords; base cases are verified by Magma computations and, for ternary cases, by exact constraint solving with Z3.

title: Local Pair Correlations And Network Geometry Govern Collective Oscillations In Nonreciprocal Ising Networks
authors: Zihua Liu, Xudong Wu, Liantuan Xiao
abstract: ArXiv:2609.13996v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nonreciprocal many-body dynamics can develop a swap phase characterized by spontaneous global oscillations far from equilibrium. To determine how local nonreciprocal interactions predict global oscillations and how broadly this prediction applies, we compare mean-field theory, independent-node theory, and nearest-neighbor spin-coupling theory for a two-spin nonreciprocal Ising model on networks of fixed coordination number (\(z=4\)). Nearest-neighbor spin-coupling theory retains nine independent joint edge probabilities. Monte Carlo benchmarks show that it predicts the oscillation amplitude, angular momentum, and period on edge-swapped networks with a 2.1\% aggregate mean absolute relative error. We then extend the square lattice to degree-preserving edge-swapped networks and find sharply different behavior. With increasing system size, the oscillation amplitude and angular momentum decay strongly on the periodic square lattice but remain nearly size independent on edge-swapped networks. These results show that identical local parameters do not determine the macroscopic phase. The contrasting finite-size trends identify network geometry as a key determinant of collective oscillations at fixed local interaction parameters.
tldr: Local pair correlations and network geometry, not identical local interaction parameters, govern the collective oscillation (swap) phase in nonreciprocal Ising networks.
motivation: Nonreciprocal many-body dynamics can spontaneously produce global oscillations far from equilibrium, but it is unclear how local nonreciprocal interactions predict macroscopic oscillations and how broadly such predictions hold.
method: The authors compare mean-field theory, independent-node theory, and a nearest-neighbor spin-coupling theory that retains nine independent joint edge probabilities, benchmarking against Monte Carlo simulations on z=4 nonreciprocal Ising networks including degree-preserving edge-swapped variants.
result: The nearest-neighbor spin-coupling theory predicts oscillation amplitude, angular momentum, and period on edge-swapped networks with 2.1% aggregate mean absolute relative error, and reveals that amplitude and angular momentum decay strongly with system size on periodic square lattices but remain nearly size independent on edge-swapped networks.
conclusion: Identical local parameters do not determine the macroscopic phase; network geometry is identified as a key determinant of collective oscillations at fixed local interaction parameters.

title: Microscopic Parametric Correlations And Spectral Rigidity In The Non-Hermitian Threefold Way
authors: Yan V Fyodorov
abstract: ArXiv:2609.13434v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study microscopic spectral correlations between two nearby parameter values in the three non-Hermitian Gaussian bulk classes: [MATH] (unconstrained), [MATH] (complex symmetric), and [MATH] (complex self-dual, with each degenerate doublet counted once). Parameter dependence is modelled by stationary matrix Ornstein--Uhlenbeck evolution, whose microscopic time scale is [MATH].
